items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: But the concert we’re going to give for example, this Friday, with Dr. Michael Woods, we, at a rehearsal, talked about the “Flower Drum Song,”

ctx.x: Well I think perhaps what you’re suggesting is that there is maybe another transformation with the younger generation? I performed with Cui Jian who is the rock icon of China — China’s first rock icon I should say. As a result I had nothing but my name. He expressed © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

the collective feelings of his generation, you know Tiananmen Square was like 1989. And next year will be the 25th anniversary. But Cui Jian expressed the sentiments of those young students at that time, who felt alienated from the cultural revolution. And so the 1980’s was the emergence of rock, but there wasn’t, you know rock represented rebellion, I guess, of the government. And so it was an expression of that but not necessarily — there was a motivation to think of yourself as an artist and trying to develop…

then I had gone through, to me, the change of tradition, the tradition of transformation in China. That “Flower Drum Song” became an important cultural device for the Chinese communist party to recruit illiterate peasants in the countryside. You’d have a performance of the “Flower Drum Song” that was something familiar to peasants to draw them in, and then later on, in 1945, [s/l] Yuan Nin, who was an actress from Shanghai and also a member of the communist party, performed it in, I think it was March of 1945…
